name: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
study_type: ground laboratory experiments (ozone-sensitized counterflow flames) and numerical modeling, using ISS FLEX data from PSI as reference
project_scientist: Daniel L. Dietrich (NASA GRC), listed as Technical Point of Contact
investigators_note: Co-Investigator: Christopher B. Reuter (Princeton University). Frequent co-authors on the listed publications: Omar R. Yehia, Sang Hee Won, Mengni Zhou, Eric Lin and Tanvir I. Farouk.
objective: Using FLEX flight data from PSI, run new simulations and ground experiments with ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to: (1) build a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusion cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion and convection; (2) connect the flammability and extinction limits of hot and cool flames; (3) verify phenomena seen in the ISS FLEX experiments; (4) obtain quantitative data on extinction limits, flame temperature and species distributions to validate kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames; (5) extend cool-flame studies from ISS droplets to a more general one-dimensional ground system with radiation, diffusion, convection and low-temperature chemistry.
hypothesis: Oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion and convection control the transition from hot flames to cool flames; the investigation asks which conditions cause this transition and how the cool-flame flammable region relates to the hot-flame flammability and extinction limits.
approach: Using the FLEX flight conditions, the effect of oxygen concentration on cool-flame extinction limits was compared with three numerical schemes: (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of an n-heptane/air mixture; (b) one-dimensional freely propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method; (c) cool-flame regimes and burning limits of DME/air at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm). Ground measurements used ozone-sensitized counterflow flames (per the objectives and the experimental table). Details are in the publications 'Dynamics of cool flames' (doi 10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787), 'Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames' (doi 10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019) and 'Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction' (doi 10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028).
geometry: one-dimensional counterflow (opposed-jet) diffusion flames; numerical one-dimensional freely propagating and spark-assisted flames
conditions_note: Oxygen concentration was varied but values are not given on the record. The 20 atm (about 294 psi) maximum applies to the DME/air simulations; pressures of the laboratory experiments are not given.
flow: counterflow (opposed jets); strain rates not given on the record
gravity_note: ground laboratory and numerical study; results compared with ISS FLEX microgravity data
hardware_note: Counterflow burner at Princeton University; formaldehyde (CH2O) planar laser-induced fluorescence and thermometry are listed in the experimental table.

sensors: thermometry (method not given on the record)

flammability and burning limits of hot, warm and cool flames (computed)

key_results: The warm diffusion flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames.
At elevated pressure the flammable region of warm and cool flames expands, because low- and intermediate-temperature reactivity increases with pressure.
Since many real engines operate at 20 to 40 atm, cool and warm flames are relevant flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion.
space_benefits: Warm and cool diffusion flames matter in microgravity because of the long residence times possible there; the work helps explain how flames move between hot, warm and cool regimes near extinction, which relates to the FLEX observations on the ISS.
earth_benefits: Relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flows and to high-pressure near-limit combustion in engines (20 to 40 atm); the calculations advance understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and guide experiments on different flame regimes.
scenario_relevance: NOT FILLED IN (to be computed from the team's ranking rules). Note: ground study of gas and vaporized fuels in counterflow flames at normal gravity, with simulations up to 20 atm; oxygen levels are not given, so it cannot be placed against lunar base conditions here. Informs cool-flame and extinction models rather than material selection.
